title: What Has Embodied Cognition Got to Do With Cognitive Load Theory
author: Dynamic Learning
summary: This piece unpacks a 2026 preprint by Gibson, Azukas, and Soylu that attempts to integrate embodied cognition theory with cognitive load theory (CLT), two research traditions that appear at first to have little in common. The author traces the connection back to earlier work by John Sweller and Fred Paas on the 'human movement effect,' which shows that watching someone perform an action activates some of the same cortical circuits as performing it, and asks whether this relatively effortless biological capacity can be recruited to ease the acquisition of hard, school-taught knowledge. Drawing on research into gestures and physical object manipulation, the article shows that meaningful hand movement and manipulatives can carry information and externalize relationships that would otherwise have to be held entirely in working memory, effectively reducing cognitive load rather than adding to it. The piece closes by summarizing the preprint's core reframe: CLT asks how much a learner is trying to hold in working memory, while embodied cognition asks how much a learner actually needs to hold, given what their body and environment are already doing for them — while noting plainly that the paper is a speculative theoretical model, not an empirical study.
points: The 'human movement effect' (Sweller and Paas) shows that watching someone perform an action activates some of the same cortical circuits as performing it yourself, raising the question of whether this low-effort biological capacity can be recruited to ease learning of cognitively demanding academic content.

Contrary to what the transient information effect would predict, animations of human movement outperform static images for learning motor procedures such as knot-tying or origami, because observing dynamic movement appears to impose less working-memory load than expected.

Meaningful gestures function as an external representational medium that carries information visuospatially rather than verbally — studies cited show children learn mathematical equivalence and conservation concepts better, and solve more problems correctly, when gesture accompanies verbal explanation.

Physical or imagined object manipulation (as in Glenberg's 'Moved by Reading' research, where children act out sentences with toy objects) produced substantially better comprehension than simply rereading text, and the benefit held even when manipulation was only imagined or done on a computer, not with real objects.

The preprint reframes cognitive load theory and embodied cognition as descriptions of the same dynamic system operating at different timescales — fast sensorimotor loops versus working-memory processes lasting seconds/minutes versus schemas developing over hours to years — and treats schemas themselves as dynamic 'attractor landscapes' rather than static stored objects, though the author is careful to note the paper is speculative, not empirical.
quotes: Put crudely, if I watch someone playing tennis, my tennis playing circuits fire.

Paas and Sweller then posed a question that went something like: can we recruit relatively effortless biologically primary processes (the human movement effect) to help us acquire cognitively demanding biological secondary knowledge?
Indeed, experiments involving origami, knot-tying, and puzzle rings support the prediction that observing dynamic human movement leads to better learning than static representations.
Gesture represents information visuospatially rather than verbally, providing additional access routes for information.
This resulted in substantially better comprehension than simply rereading the sentences.

While CLT might ask: How much information is the learner trying to hold in working memory? Embodied cognition asks: How much information does the learner actually need to hold in working memory, given what their body and the environment are doing for them?
The authors reject the notion of schemas as static objects stored in long-term memory and awaiting retrieval. They are dynamic attractor landscapes.
This isn't an empirical study, but a proposed model for integrating embodied cognition with cognitive load theory.
